title: IPOC: An Adaptive Interval Prediction Model based on Online Chasing and Conformal Inference for Large-Scale Systems

problem.claim: Accurate prediction is difficult in large-scale systems because system complexity, demand volatility, and diverse dynamic workloads create challenging prediction conditions.

gap.claim: The work addresses the online interval prediction problem for large-scale, real-time workload streams.

contributions.claim: The authors propose IPOC, a lightweight and flexible model for producing confidence intervals while adapting to real-time workload-stream dynamics.
The authors formulate ensemble learning for online interval prediction as a dynamic deterministic Markov Decision Process and convert it into a stateful online learning task.
IPOC selects a target model at each time and applies a designed chasing oracle to produce confidence intervals.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that, to their knowledge, this is the first application of frontier online-learning theory to time-series prediction tasks.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report theoretical validation through sublinear regret analysis and satisfaction of confidence-interval requirements.
The authors report extensive experiments on four real-world datasets comparing IPOC with 19 baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: Large-scale systems contain complex, volatile, diverse, and dynamic workloads that make accurate prediction difficult.
The work formulates an online interval prediction problem and uses ensemble learning to address it.
The ensemble-learning problem is represented as a dynamic deterministic Markov Decision Process and recast as a stateful online learning task.
IPOC produces adaptive confidence intervals by selecting target models and applying a chasing oracle to real-time workload streams.
The authors report theoretical analysis and experiments on four real-world datasets against 19 baselines.

source_observation.claim: The approach models changing ensemble decisions as a stateful online-learning problem and adapts target-model selection over time.

interpretation.claim: When prediction conditions and workload streams evolve, explicitly modeling temporal decision dynamics may support more adaptive uncertainty estimation.

application.claim: Consider online-learning formulations and adaptive model selection for interval prediction in changing production workloads.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish performance outside the reported datasets, baselines, or workload conditions.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the confidence-interval metrics, coverage targets, or regret bounds.
The abstract does not identify the four datasets, 19 baselines, or comparative results.
The abstract does not provide implementation details, computational costs, or deployment constraints.
